categoryNotes.story: Concrete, dated examples for behavioural questions ('tell me about a time'). Deliberately separated from experience so retrieval doesn't surface 2007 anecdotes when someone asks what Chris does now. Always keep the date in the text.

chunks.title: Who Chris is
chunks.text: Chris Pollard is a Melbourne-based AI delivery lead — a hands-on engineer who also brings a decade of project and product management. He builds production LLM systems himself, with a solo-built multi-agent platform as his flagship, and can own delivery end to end: roadmap and stakeholders through to shipped, working software.

chunks.title: What makes Chris's profile rare
chunks.text: What's rare is the pairing. Most AI hires are strong on the build or strong on delivery; Chris does both — writing the agents and the retrieval, and landing the project with the people around it. He keeps a human at the edge of every automated decision, and cares that what ships is trustworthy and actually used. He is based in Melbourne, Australia.

chunks.title: Bitcoin Treasury Solutions — Director
chunks.text: Bitcoin Treasury Solutions — Director (March 2025 to present, Melbourne). This is Chris's current role. The business delivers structured bitcoin training for professionals, SMEs and individuals, and it is also where his production AI work sits: business-mono, the multi-agent operations platform he architected and built solo in TypeScript on Mastra, Next.js 15 and Supabase with pgvector, runs the operation day to day.

chunks.title: Juvare — Technical Implementation Analyst
chunks.text: Juvare — Technical Implementation Analyst (December 2023 to May 2026, Melbourne). The title understates the shape of it: roughly 70% front-end web development, 20% business analysis and 10% direct client work. The product is WebEOC, Juvare's emergency and incident management platform; the company is US-owned with core server-side development based in Lithuania, so the Australian team operated as the client-facing end of a distributed product organisation. Chris mentored newer developers both locally and remotely, helped supervise onboarding, and led the implementation of a code-review system.

chunks.title: Beyond Essential Systems — Software Engineer
chunks.text: Beyond Essential Systems — Software Engineer (September 2021 to December 2023, Melbourne). Full-stack development across server- and client-side packages in a monorepo, including microservices and a React Native app. Contributed to Tupaia, an open-source health-data aggregation and visualisation platform for low-resource settings, and Tamanu, an electronic medical record system for the Pacific region.

chunks.title: General Assembly — Software Engineering Immersive
chunks.text: General Assembly — Software Engineering Immersive (2021, Melbourne). A 12-week full-time programme covering JavaScript, Node.js (Express), React, REST APIs, Ruby/Sinatra, PostgreSQL and Git — Chris's structured transition from product management into software engineering.

chunks.title: VTAC — Project Manager (product)
chunks.text: Victorian Tertiary Admissions Centre — Project Manager (November 2014 to March 2020, Melbourne). Owned delivery of the FlexiDirect SaaS platform — the direct application portal used by education providers — as product manager, from client discovery and pricing model to roadmap and release, coordinating developers, testers and UX designers to ship against strategic goals. The clearest early example of Chris leading technical delivery end to end.

chunks.title: Earlier career (2007–2021)
chunks.text: Before software, Chris spent over a decade leading projects, coordinating teams and managing stakeholders — including pandemic-response project management at RMIT University, project coordination at La Trobe, and student-administration roles at Monash, the University of Melbourne and Swinburne. It's where the delivery-and-stakeholder half of his skill set was built.

chunks.title: Education and certifications
chunks.text: Bachelor of Performing Arts, Monash University (2004–2007); Graduate Diploma in Education, La Trobe University (2009–2010); Software Engineering Immersive, General Assembly (2021). Certifications include WebEOC Bootcamp, a Bitcoin Protocol Development seminar series, and freelance website development.

chunks.title: business-mono — overview
chunks.text: business-mono is a production multi-agent operations platform Chris built single-handedly as the system behind Bitcoin Treasury Solutions, where he is Director. It uses a hub-and-spoke design: a coordinator agent (Simon) is the only agent that talks to humans and routes work to specialists, all sharing one Supabase database. A Mastra server runs the agents and workflows; a Next.js 15 app handles dashboards and human approvals.

chunks.title: Hub-and-spoke coordination
chunks.text: Rather than a flat swarm, a single coordinator routes each request to the right specialist agent — recorder, archivist, project manager, business analyst, content, research, relationship and compliance roles — behind a consistent audit trail. Centralising human contact in the coordinator keeps behaviour predictable and the whole system observable.

chunks.title: Hybrid retrieval
chunks.text: The knowledge base uses hybrid search rather than a single vector lookup: pgvector (HNSW) similarity, graph traversal across knowledge connections, and Postgres full-text search, so each query uses the method that fits it. Embeddings are generated with OpenAI text-embedding-3-small at 1536 dimensions.

chunks.title: Suspend / resume elicitation
chunks.text: The requirements workflow runs multi-round clarification loops using Mastra's suspend and resume: it pauses mid-workflow to ask a human for input, then resumes with that answer folded in. This is structured elicitation with state carried across turns, not a single hopeful prompt.

chunks.title: Approval graduation model
chunks.text: Operations earn autonomy in stages: an action moves from human-confirmed, to batch-approved, to autonomous as it proves reliable. High-risk actions — outbound emails, published content and CRM writes — stay human-approved regardless of track record. Trust is graduated, not granted.

chunks.title: Compliance gate in the loop
chunks.text: A dedicated compliance agent reviews advice-framed drafts against Australian financial-services (AFSL) rules, records its verdict and never auto-approves. If the copy changes, the review re-runs — governance is wired into the workflow rather than left to a final human glance.

chunks.title: Ingestion and interfaces
chunks.text: The platform ingests real-world inputs through several channels — a Signal messaging interface for directors, plus telephony and meeting sources — with speech transcription feeding the same knowledge base the agents retrieve from. Inputs become searchable context, closing the loop between what happens and what the agents know.

chunks.title: Deployment and structure
chunks.text: The codebase is a Turborepo monorepo. Agents and workflows run on Railway; the Next.js web app deploys to Vercel; Supabase provides Postgres and pgvector. A Vitest suite, including agent evals, is gated in CI.

chunks.title: Core stack
chunks.text: Chris works primarily in TypeScript and Node.js. On the web he uses Next.js 15 (App Router), React and React Native; for agents and workflows, Mastra; and Supabase with pgvector for data and retrieval, organised in a Turborepo monorepo. His full-stack background spans microservices and client apps. He writes end-to-end and integration tests as part of the work, not after it.

chunks.title: LLM engineering skills
chunks.text: On the LLM side he builds agent orchestration, retrieval-augmented generation, hybrid search, tool use and human-in-the-loop control flow, and treats evals as first-class, gated in CI. His production agent work is built on Mastra; he has also prototyped pipelines with Flowise and LangChain.

chunks.title: Scale and ownership
chunks.text: business-mono is a genuinely solo build: the coordinator, the specialist agents, the workflows, the ingestion pipelines and the web app were all architected and shipped by one person, across a Turborepo monorepo with a CI-gated eval suite. It has been under sustained development rather than built in a burst, and it runs a real business daily. The repository is public, so the scope can be inspected rather than taken on trust.

chunks.title: How Chris works
chunks.text: Chris works docs-first — per-agent specifications, a design brief and a defined brand voice sit alongside the code — and brings design thinking to systems, not just interfaces. Evals gate changes in CI, so behaviour is verified rather than assumed.

chunks.title: How much experience does he have?
chunks.text: Chris pairs a decade of project and product delivery with hands-on engineering. He moved into software in 2021 — full-stack roles at Beyond Essential Systems and Juvare — and now builds multi-agent LLM systems, so he can both make the technical calls and lead the delivery.

chunks.title: Has he shipped to production?
chunks.text: Yes. business-mono is a live, deployed multi-agent system running real operations, not a demo — built and shipped solo, with agents on Railway, the web app on Vercel and a CI-gated test suite.

chunks.title: How does it stay safe?
chunks.text: Through layered controls: approval graduation (human-confirmed to autonomous as trust is earned), always-human gates on emails, published content and CRM writes, and a compliance agent that reviews regulated advice and never auto-approves.

chunks.title: Where is he based / remote?
chunks.text: Chris is based in Melbourne, Australia. He's open to fully remote roles and to hybrid work within Melbourne, but isn't currently looking to relocate.

chunks.title: Is he available?
chunks.text: Chris is available now for part-time and fractional engagements, and has full contract capacity from mid-2027. He finished at Juvare in May 2026 and directs Bitcoin Treasury Solutions, so until then the shape of the engagement matters as much as the role. He's particularly interested in AI delivery lead work.

chunks.title: VTAC — building and leading the project management office
chunks.text: Alongside managing product at VTAC, Chris ran the project management office, which he grew from one person to six full-time staff between 2018 and 2020. He set the practice up as well as staffing it: documentation standards, risk and change management, and coordination across developers, testers and UX. It is the clearest example of him leading people, not just delivery.

chunks.title: Chris on listening
chunks.text: A principle Chris has stated consistently across his career: he listens more than he talks, and pays as much attention to what people aren't saying as to what they are. His view is that most people already know the right decision — they need a safe enough room to articulate it. It's why elicitation and human-in-the-loop design keep showing up in the systems he builds.

chunks.title: Chris on owning decisions
chunks.text: The second principle he returns to: don't just make decisions, own them — including the wrong ones. His argument is that visible ownership of mistakes is a net positive for the individual, the team and the organisation, because it lets the team learn and sets a norm of honesty. Easy to say, he notes, and hard to actually do.

chunks.title: Working between engineers and non-technical stakeholders
chunks.text: Chris has spent years as the person in the middle: at VTAC the development team worked in Agile while the university clients expected a waterfall shape, and his job was to find a working balance rather than force either side to convert. He writes user stories, runs discovery, and translates technical constraint into terms a client can make decisions with. Recruiters asking whether he can face a client as well as a codebase have a decade of evidence for it.

chunks.title: Senior stakeholder relationships
chunks.text: Through the VTAC years Chris built and held relationships with senior executives across Victorian universities and education providers — a consortium environment where clients are also owners, and competing interests are the normal condition rather than an exception. He handled client discovery and pricing as well as delivery, so the commercial conversation and the technical one sat with the same person.

chunks.title: Example — growing a project office from one to six
chunks.text: Example (VTAC, 2018–2020). Chris took a project management office that was one person — him — and grew it to six full-time staff over two years, defining how the practice worked as it scaled: documentation, risk and change management, and how project managers interfaced with an in-house full-stack team building both B2C and B2B applications. Useful answer to 'has he built anything beyond his own output?'

chunks.title: Example — reconciling Agile delivery with waterfall clients
chunks.text: Example (VTAC, FlexiDirect application portal). The internal development team ran Agile; the university and provider clients planned in waterfall, with fixed annual admissions deadlines they could not move. Rather than convert either side, Chris ran the project as a translation layer — iterative internally, milestone-shaped externally — so engineers kept their cadence and clients kept the commitments they needed. Good answer to questions about conflicting stakeholder expectations.

chunks.title: Example — delivering to a hard external deadline alone
chunks.text: Example (Global Vision Media, 2007). On a four-person team producing a community television pilot series, Chris shot, edited and compiled each episode for ingest by Channel 31 at the end of every week — mostly working solo in the edit suite with minimal direction. An early instance of the pattern that shows up again in business-mono: given a deadline and no supervision, the thing ships.

chunks.title: Is he good with people and stakeholders?
chunks.text: It's the half of the profile most AI engineers don't have. A decade of project and product roles — VTAC, La Trobe, RMIT, Monash, Melbourne, Swinburne — was spent facing clients, executives, academics and students, and the current work carries it forward: client discovery, requirements elicitation, and designing systems that keep a human in the decision. He'd rather run the awkward conversation early than discover the misalignment at delivery.

chunks.title: Has he led a team?
chunks.text: Yes, though it's worth being precise about which kind. He built and led VTAC's project management office growing it from one person to six between 2018 and 2020, and at Juvare he mentored newer developers locally and remotely, supervised onboarding, and led the rollout of a code-review system. business-mono, by contrast, is a solo build — the evidence there is architectural ownership and the ability to carry a whole system alone, not headcount.

chunks.title: Why did he move from project management into engineering?
chunks.text: Working alongside VTAC's in-house development team is what did it — managing a software product from the non-technical side made him want to build rather than only coordinate. He formalised the move deliberately through General Assembly's immersive in 2021 and went straight into full-stack engineering. He didn't leave delivery behind so much as add the other half to it.

chunks.title: Why bitcoin?
chunks.text: It's a long-running interest rather than a recent turn — he was following the protocol closely by 2019, running a bitcoin-core full node and experimenting with lightning by 2021, and completed a protocol development seminar series. Bitcoin Treasury Solutions grew out of that, and its main relevance here is that it gave him a real business with real compliance obligations to build production agents against. His personal bitcoin projects sit under the dragon-foobar GitHub account.

chunks.title: Beyond Essential — developer education on Tupaia map configuration (first months)
chunks.text: For his first few months at Beyond Essential Systems, Chris was assigned to developer education — an informal remit rather than a title — for a new visual tool in Tupaia that let non-engineers configure map overlays, working closely with the JSON configuration underneath it. He wrote most of the tool's documentation and onboarded the data analysts who became its primary users, raising issues and improvements as he taught it and then building them himself. He moved into full-stack engineering across the wider codebase from there.

chunks.title: Teaching the tool, then fixing what the teaching exposes
chunks.text: A pattern that recurs in Chris's work: get the users onto the tool, write the documentation, and treat the places they get stuck as the product backlog. At Beyond Essential he onboarded data analysts onto a new map configuration tool in Tupaia and wrote most of its docs, which meant he saw the friction first-hand and could turn it into issues and improvements he then implemented. It is the forward-deployed loop — sit with the users, find what is breaking, ship the fix — rather than collecting feedback and handing it to someone else.

chunks.title: Where to find his code
chunks.text: Chris's code sits across three GitHub accounts, and they do different jobs. avunculargroup is the current one and the one to look at — business-mono and his AI work live there. chris-pollard is the earlier professional account, covering his Beyond Essential Systems work from 2021 to 2023; Tupaia and Tamanu are both public repositories under the beyondessential organisation, so that work is open to inspection — his commits are filterable by author in the Tupaia repository rather than sitting as repos on his own profile. dragon-foobar holds personal projects.

chunks.title: Can I see code he has actually written?
chunks.text: Yes, and without needing anyone's permission. His Beyond Essential commits are public in the Tupaia repository and filterable by author, covering 2021 to 2023 on an open-source platform used for health data in low-resource settings. business-mono, the multi-agent platform, sits under the avunculargroup account. Between them: two years of team engineering in a shared production codebase, and a complete system architected and shipped solo.

chunks.title: Visual craft and design taste
chunks.text: Chris came into software from a visual discipline: a performing arts degree, then six years running his own video production business through to 2011 — shooting, editing and delivering for paying clients — including a stint as camera operator and editor on a broadcast series. It left him with a trained eye rather than a decorative one, and it showed in the front-end work he did at Juvare and in how he approaches interface and information design. It is also why design thinking reads as a habit in his work rather than borrowed vocabulary. Running that business — quoting, budgeting, delivering — is the same shape as the fractional engagements he takes now.

chunks.title: Beyond Essential — what he actually built
chunks.text: On Tupaia, Chris built graph and map visualisation features — the charts and geographic overlays that turn aggregated health data into something a decision-maker can read — along with the admin panel UI used to configure them. He also worked on the underlying database structure, built REST APIs and server-side microservices to serve that data, and wrote end-to-end tests across the stack. This is ordinary product engineering in a shared codebase with other engineers, which is the one thing a solo project cannot evidence.

chunks.title: Juvare — government clients and requirements work
chunks.text: At Juvare (December 2023 to May 2026), Chris's clients were Australian and New Zealand government agencies at state level, ranging from police through to primary industries. The work was to sit with them, understand their requirements and business processes, and tailor WebEOC into applications that fit how they actually operate — the systems these agencies rely on during incidents. It was forward-deployed work in all but name — the same person ran the discovery conversation and built the result.

chunks.title: Juvare — building inside legacy constraints
chunks.text: Parts of WebEOC run on older technology — jQuery and legacy JavaScript bundles — so building for a client meant working creatively within the limits of the platform rather than reaching for a rewrite. Chris also experimented with introducing web components as a way to modernise incrementally. Relevant to anyone hiring into an established codebase rather than a blank repository.
